newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's Telefonica offer attractive despite crowd.
newsitem.headline: Spain's Telefonica offer attractive despite crowd.

text.p: Spain's rush to privatise telecoms operator Telefonica puts one of the state's most valuable holdings into a flooded market but analysts believe it will still prove attractive.

The government confirmed on Monday it was selling its remaining 21.2 percent share early next year -- squeezing it in among other European telecom privatisations from Germany this month, Italy in March and France in April.
But sector analysts were not bothered by the competition, saying the Spanish operator's Latin American holdings made it unique among the Europeans.
"Spain's offer of Telefonica is very attractive," Jaime Smith of Benito y Monjardin said. "Its strong position in Latin America makes it different from other telecoms."
Telefonica started building up contacts in the fast-growing Latin American countries in the early 1990s, when the economies there had appeared to stabilise.

The operator bet strongly on its ability to do business in the Spanish speaking world and used its international subsidiary TISA to buy up fledgling operators and bid for licenses in untouched or newly opened markets.
It now has considerable, profit-generating holdings in Chile, Argentina and Peru and stakes in operators in Mexico, Venezuela, Colombia, Puerto Rico, Brazil and the United States.
TISA, which had a 17 percent gain in profits last year from 1994, generated 22 percent of Telefonica's overall earnings of 133 billion pesetas ($1 billion).
Another positive factor for Telefonica in investor eyes is its ability to face competition when the market is fully liberalised after 1998.

Spain has been progressively opening up niche markets in the telecommunications sector since 1987, giving Telefonica ample time to adjust to the competition and analysts believe most negative effects have already been factored into the share price.
"Full liberalisation could even be beneficial to Telefonica," one said, adding that the telecoms market was much more of a known animal than say the electricity sector.
Analysts expect the government could earn some 500 billion pesetas from the share offer, even if placed at a time of heavy competition.
"It's not the best moment, but it doesn't seem to be too bad," said Ignacio Cornejo of brokers Beta Bolsa in Madrid. "Telefonica is certainly attractive at these prices."

Telefonica shares were quoting 15 pesetas higher at 2,470 at midday on Tuesday. They took an initial hit on Friday as rumours of the share offer started to circulate, but then quickly rallied as the market digested the news.

"It's true there are a lot of telecoms being placed on the market, but the bourse is at high levels right now and depending on when the offer is made, there could be a good amount of interest," Cornejo said.
Analysts in London approved of the decision to rush the Spanish operator onto the market, saying the timing gave it an advantage over other later European privatisations.
Apart from generating international interest, local analysts said there was enough domestic interest, both institutional and retail, to absorb Spain's heavy schedule of privatisations.
The conservative government also plans to raise cash by selling off its remaining stakes in banking group Argentaria, electricity utility Endesa and energy firm Repsol.

"There's some disillusionment in the market as the investment funds have turned out to be less profitable than foreseen," Smith said. "These share offers are a good alternative." ($ = 129.2 Spanish Pesetas)
